title: Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0130】Therefore, this review aims to inventory the cardiac side effects of thoracic radiotherapy, assess their relationship with radiation dose to cardiac/pulmonary structures and assess their impact on survival.

【Introduction · p0115】Radiotherapy plays an important role in the curative treatment of (locally advanced) thoracic malignancies [1], [2], [3], [4]. Radiotherapy improves survival and tumour control by inducing direct and indirect DNA damage, leading to cancer cell death [5], [6]. However, inevitable radiation exposure of heart and lungs may lead to cardiac side effects [7], [8]. These include myocardial fibrosis, reduced cardiac systolic function, coronary artery diseases, pericarditis, arrhythmia, and valvular disorders [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]. These side effects can significantly impact quality of life, and even survival, thereby partly compromising the benefits of radiotherapy [12], [13].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methods · p0140】Studies were included if they: (1) involved adult patients with thoracic cancers treated with radiotherapy; (2) analysed radiation dose to organs at risk; (3) reported cardiac side effects separately; and (4) were published in English. Exclusion criteria included stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, case studies, editorials, meeting abstracts, and reviews. Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy was excluded because of its very high doses per fraction over a shorter treatment course, expected to result in dose-effect relationships that differ significantly from those occurring in conventional radiotherapy [24].

【Methods · p0145】The search strategy included terms related to thoracic malignities, radiotherapy dose, and cardiac side effects and is available in the Supplementary Table 1. Title/abstract screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and data extraction were performed by a single reviewer (UF), using Rayyan [25]. Fig. 1 summarizes the study selection process, including duplicate removal and reasons for full-text exclusion. Extracted data included study characteristics (e.g., publication year, patient population, follow-up length, and study endpoints), cardiac dose parameters, and their associations with cardiac outcomes and survival. Supplementary Table 2 summarizes the characteristics and main findings of the included studies, including reported effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals where available. In accordance with the objectives of this scoping review and PRISMA-ScR, no formal risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies was performed.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · p0360】Thoracic radiotherapy inevitably exposes portions of the heart and lungs to radiation. Accumulating evidence suggests that such exposure can affect cardiac structures and functions resulting in a broad spectrum of cardiac side effects. Furthermore, radiation dose to both cardiac and pulmonary tissues has been associated with reduced overall survival. As radiotherapy techniques continue to improve, minimizing radiation exposure to critical cardiopulmonary structures is becoming increasingly achievable. The findings of this review suggest that such dose reductions may not only decrease the risk of treatment-related toxicity but also contribute to improved long-term outcomes for patients undergoing thoracic radiotherapy.

【Valvular heart disease · p0185】Valvular heart disease is common after radiotherapy, with e.g., a prevalence of 30-50% among lymphoma patients within 10-20 year after treatment [[64], [65], [66], [67], [68]]. Association with radiation dose to the heart, or more specifically the valves (Supplementary Table 2), suggest that radiotherapy plays a role in this [[64], [65], [66], [67], [68], [69]]. Only one study did not find a relationship with dose, likely due to a low number of valvular disease events observed (n = 3) [70]. Most of these studies were performed in lymphoma patients, likely due to the long latency of valvular disease exceeding the typical life expectancy of patients with lung or oesophageal cancer [[71], [72], [73]].
